current_answer: The U.S. early-career warning is stronger, but the causal fight is harder. Census hiring and graduate records, plus a revised Stanford analysis of ADP payroll data, all find weaker outcomes for young workers in more AI-exposed work; Stanford puts the 22–25 employment gap at 19% relative to less-exposed peers. That is not a causal verdict: the Stanford authors call it descriptive, and a new cross-country paper finds remote-work exposure can absorb much of a similar junior-hiring pattern. Broad U.S. postings still show little distinct AI-driven decline. Watch entry routes closely; do not call the whole job market lost.

catalogue_card.question: Is the 19% AI job gap real?
catalogue_card.text: A revised payroll study finds a larger early-career gap. A new remote-work challenge means the AI verdict is still open.

summary: A revised Stanford analysis of ADP payroll data finds U.S. workers aged 22–25 in highly AI-exposed occupations were about 19% below the employment level they would have reached by keeping pace with less-exposed peers through June 2026; experienced workers did not show a comparable gap.
The authors call the pattern descriptive, not causal. They report pre-existing trends, education differences, sample-representativeness limits and sensitivity when overall firm hiring is controlled.

Two U.S. Census studies separately find lower early-career hires, initial employment and earnings in more AI-exposed industry-state cells or college majors. They also use exposure rather than observed employer adoption.

A University of Warwick working paper finds remote-work exposure remains predictive of lower junior hiring and limited-experience ads after joint estimation, while its generative-AI coefficient often attenuates to no statistical distinction from zero.
A Federal Reserve analysis still finds little indication of a distinct AI-driven fall in broad U.S. job postings. That measure does not settle actual hires or entry outcomes.
AI use is broader than a simple occupation score but shallow in most tasks and occupations, so exposure, adoption and labor outcomes must remain separate.
uncertainty: No current study can tell a reader whether their own job will be lost to AI.

The central early-career findings are exposure-based, not observed-adoption experiments. Remote work, education, pre-trends, other simultaneous shocks and sample selection remain live attribution problems.
Employment, hires, postings, initial earnings, hours and task use are different outcomes that can move differently.
freshness_note: Updated 14 September 2026 after a revised ADP payroll analysis and a new cross-country remote-work attribution challenge. We will revise when monitored sources, later cohorts or observed-adoption studies change the balance.
